units.title: A person cannot simultaneously hold a Nebraska driving permit or license and a state identification card.
A Nebraska license or State ID Card issued to a person with lawful status is limited to the authorized U.S. stay, or to one year if that stay has no definite end.
Nebraska will not issue a license while driving privileges are suspended or revoked in any state or jurisdiction.
Suspension temporarily removes a person’s valid license and driving privilege.
Revocation removes the driving privilege and takes the license for a specified period.
A suspension or revocation continues until the driver satisfies reinstatement requirements and pays required fees.
Impoundment means a court holds the license and prohibits driving for the ordered period.
Confiscation means an officer seizes the license after an alcohol-test failure or refusal.
After confiscation, the issued temporary license lasts fifteen days.
At the end of the fifteen-day temporary license after alcohol-test failure or refusal, the license is revoked unless a departmental hearing dismisses the violation.
A motor-vehicle homicide can cause loss of a license.
Repeated traffic violations in any state can cause loss of driving privileges.
Using a vehicle to commit a crime can lead to license loss.
A drug- or alcohol-impaired-driving arrest or conviction can lead to license loss.
Falsifying or concealing application information can lead to license loss.
Leaving a crash without providing a name and address can lead to license loss.
Ignoring a citation or court judgment in Nebraska or another state can lead to license loss.
Alcoholism or drug addiction can lead to loss of driving privileges.
Flight from an officer to avoid arrest can lead to license loss.
Refusing a chemical test can lead to license loss.
Reckless driving can lead to loss of the license.
Lending a driver license to another person can lead to license loss.
Having another person take the licensing test can lead to license loss.
A conviction for failing to show insurance proof can lead to license loss.
Failure to comply with a child-support or alimony order can lead to license loss.
A driver younger than twenty-one can lose driving privileges for failing to complete required improvement training after accumulating six points in a year.
Transporting a child while intoxicated can lead to license loss.
Violating school learner, school or learner permit terms also bars eligibility for another permit until age sixteen.
Accumulating twelve points within two years automatically revokes the operator license for six months.
The DMV’s point-revocation letter directs the driver to surrender the license.
Failure to surrender the revoked license can bring a fine up to five hundred dollars, up to thirty days in county jail, or both.
Point-based reinstatement requires successful completion, at the driver’s expense, of a DMV-approved driver-education and training course with at least four hours of instruction.
After point revocation, financial-responsibility proof must remain in force for three years after the original revocation ends.
A second Nebraska point revocation within five years removes driving privileges for three years.
A motor-vehicle-homicide conviction carries twelve points.
A third drunk-driving offense carries twelve points.
Failure to report a crash to law enforcement carries six points.
Failure to help after a crash involving the driver carries six points.
Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs carries six points.
Willful reckless driving carries six points.
Leaving a crash scene carries six points.
Reckless driving carries five points.
Careless driving carries four points.
Failure to yield that injures a pedestrian carries four points.
Using a handheld wireless device to read, type or send written messages while driving carries three points.
Negligent driving carries three points.
Passing a school bus with its stop arm out and red lights flashing carries three points.
Failure to yield to a pedestrian without injury carries two points.
Unlawfully blocking the driver’s view carries one point.
Refusal of an alcohol-content test carries one point.
A child-restraint violation carries one point.
Financial-responsibility proof after point revocation is usually an insurer’s written certification identified as Form SR-twenty-two.
For court-ordered revocation, financial-responsibility proof is usually an insurer’s written Form SR-twenty-two certification.
The handbook assigns no points for parking violations, muffler violations or failure to carry a valid operator license on the person.
A sobriety program permit issued during the subsequent-offense or refusal waiting-period pathway is valid only for the remaining portion of the one-year administrative revocation.
A later-offense interlock permit during administrative revocation lasts for the remaining portion of that one-year revocation.
After the refusal waiting period, the interlock permit lasts only for the remaining portion of the one-year administrative revocation.

Fleeing an officer to avoid arrest or citation for a Nebraska misdemeanor or traffic infraction, or a city or village ordinance violation other than a nonmoving traffic violation, is a Class I misdemeanor and may also revoke the operator license.
For the handbook’s age-seventeen-and-younger juvenile-court offense rule, an individual without a permit or license is prohibited from obtaining one for thirty days.
For a citation dated November fourteen, two thousand twenty or later, driving one through five miles per hour above the limit adds no points inside or outside city limits.
Inside city limits, speeding more than five but no more than ten miles per hour above the limit carries two points.
Inside city limits, speeding more than ten through thirty-five miles per hour above the limit carries three points.
Speeding more than thirty-five miles per hour above the limit carries four points inside or outside city limits.
Outside city limits, speeding more than five through ten miles per hour above the limit carries one point.
Outside city limits, speeding more than ten through fifteen miles per hour above the limit carries two points.
Outside city limits, speeding more than fifteen through thirty-five miles per hour above the limit carries three points.
Driving with an expired license or without ever having received a license carries one point.
A provisional or school permit passenger violation carries one point.
A wireless-device violation under provisional, learner, school or school learner permit restrictions carries one point.
A traffic conviction adds points using the violation date rather than the conviction date.
Traffic convictions stay on the driving record for five years.
Points stop counting two years after the violation date.
An out-of-state traffic conviction receives Nebraska points as though the violation happened in Nebraska.
A driver without a CDL or CLP may receive a two-point credit after successfully completing a DMV-approved improvement course before the violation that would bring the total to twelve points.
The improvement-course point credit can be used only once every five years.
A serious traffic conviction can result in a court-ordered license revocation for the period the court specifies.
Court-ordered revocation requires financial-responsibility proof for three years after the original revocation’s ending date.
The court returns an impounded license when the impoundment period ends.
Driving during general court-ordered impoundment brings a one-year revocation upon conviction, while driving during the separately stated underage drinking or refusal impoundment brings six months.
For a driver aged twenty or younger, a conviction under the alcohol-content rule of zero point zero two percent leads to thirty days of court impoundment.
For a driver aged twenty or younger, the conviction under the zero point zero two-percent alcohol rule remains on the record for ninety days and is then deleted.
An underage refusal conviction leads to ninety days of court impoundment.
An underage refusal conviction remains on the record for one hundred twenty days and is then deleted.
A driver convicted of driving during impoundment under the underage drinking or refusal procedure receives a six-month court-ordered license revocation.
Administrative revocation permits immediate license confiscation after an alcohol-test failure or refusal of an alcohol-or-drug chemical test.
A first alcohol-test failure brings a one hundred eighty-day administrative revocation.
A later alcohol-test failure brings a year of administrative revocation.
Refusing a chemical alcohol-or-drug test brings a year of administrative revocation.
A driver subject to administrative revocation may request a hearing to challenge it.
A driver who requests an administrative-revocation hearing cannot drive with an interlock or sobriety permit until the court orders it as part of sentencing.
Waiving the administrative hearing can allow eligible driving with an ignition-interlock permit during some or all of the revocation.
A participant in the twenty-four over seven sobriety program who has a court-certified order must obtain a Sobriety Program Permit.
A sobriety program permit permits driving during administrative revocation only when the driving record otherwise allows it.
For a subsequent offense, sobriety-permit eligibility begins forty-five days after the temporary license expires.
After chemical-test refusal, sobriety-permit eligibility begins ninety days after the temporary license expires.
A sobriety program permit is revoked when the DMV receives a conviction abstract revoking driving privileges or a court order revoking that permit.
A sobriety-permit participant must be at least eighteen and have held or tested for a Class O or Class M license.
A sobriety program permit does not authorize commercial vehicle operation.
An employment drive permit after qualifying point or child-support revocation allows only direct home-and-work travel under its employment terms.
An employment drive permit does not authorize commercial vehicle operation.
An eligible first-time administrative-revocation offender may apply for an interlock permit after the temporary license’s fifteen days expire.
For a first-time offender subject to administrative license revocation, the interlock permit lasts six months and allows driving a vehicle equipped with the interlock system.
For a later administrative-revocation offense, interlock-permit eligibility begins forty-five days after temporary-license expiration.
After chemical-test refusal, interlock-permit eligibility begins ninety days after temporary-license expiration.
A court or the Board of Pardons may order interlock use for as long as fifteen years, depending on the record and prior convictions.
The base offense for a driver’s interlock tampering, circumvention or driving without the required device is a Class I misdemeanor.

The handbook describes an alcohol-related Class IV felony enhancement for a driver’s interlock tampering, circumvention or driving without the required device, but does not specify the alcohol-threshold unit.
Interlock-permit eligibility requires having held a Class O or Class M license.
After point revocation, a medical-hardship permit limits travel to trips from home or work to the specified treatment location and back.
Fleeing to avoid arrest for a felony is a Class IV felony and can also cause license revocation.
A conviction for leaving a motor-vehicle crash scene can revoke the driver license for as long as a year.
For a driver aged twenty or younger, a first minor-in-possession conviction impounds the permit or license for thirty days.
For a person aged twenty or younger, a second minor-in-possession conviction impounds the permit or license for ninety days.
For a person aged twenty or younger, a third or later minor-in-possession conviction impounds the permit or license for twelve months.

An unlicensed person aged twenty or younger cannot obtain a permit or license for thirty days after a first minor-in-possession conviction, ninety days after a second, or twelve months after a third or later conviction.
For a juvenile aged seventeen or younger, a first juvenile-court drug conviction impounds the permit or license for thirty days.
For a juvenile aged seventeen or younger, a second juvenile-court drug conviction impounds the permit or license for ninety days.
For a juvenile aged seventeen or younger, a third or later juvenile-court drug conviction impounds the permit or license for twelve months.

An unlicensed juvenile aged seventeen or younger cannot obtain a permit or license for thirty days after a first juvenile-court drug conviction, ninety days after a second, or twelve months after a third or later conviction.
For any juvenile-court offense involving a person aged seventeen or younger, the court may impound driving documents for thirty days.
A driver whose license was suspended, revoked, cancelled or disqualified must complete reinstatement before a new license can be issued.
